stories.headline: 'They smoke us': Why a moon astronaut thinks F1 is ahead of NASA
stories.summary:
150-char blurb
Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman explains why F1's engineering is ahead of NASA's, his admiration for Mercedes and what he learned on the moon.
stories.body:
Somewhere between Earth and the moon, Reid Wiseman encountered a problem. The windows of his Artemis II spacecraft were filthy.

It wasn't a mechanical failure, the haunting bleep of a master alarm or some other unforeseen consequence borne out of attempting to travel further than any human beings in history. Instead, the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission had spent so much time with their faces pressed against the glass, gazing in awe at both the diminishing Earth in one direction and the extraordinary lunar landscape growing bigger in the other, that the windows were covered in smudges.

"We were looking out at Earth and we were looking out at the moon all the time," Wiseman told ESPN. "Victor [Glover], my pilot, made a comment when we got into our first orbit of Earth, he's like, 'that's the last time Reid ever looked inside [the spacecraft].'

- Nate Saunders on the contradictions of Austin's COTA

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

- Fernando Alonso slams 'low quality bottom third of the grid'

"We had to do a photo analysis of the windows so that the geology team could make sure there was no damage, or if they were seeing blemishes on lunar photography, they could relay it back. And I was looking at the windows before I got the camera out to do the survey, and I called down to Mission Control and said, 'hey, first, I need to clean them, because the amount of grease marks from our noses and foreheads on the windows, it was just completely covered.'"

For the commander of the first crewed mission to the moon in more than half a century, it was an understandable distraction. The view was unlike anything he had experienced before, even during his previous six-month stint aboard the International Space Station.

"We're human. Making sure the spacecraft is operating is of the prime of importance. But right underneath that is absorbing the experience. The thing that struck me most looking at the Earth is it got very small, and then it got, like, that big," Wiseman said, pushing his thumb and index finger almost completely together.

"But really looking at the moon was the three-dimensionality of everything. You're not looking through an atmosphere. Everything is crystal clear, everything. The blacks, the craters, the bumps, the sun hitting the crater rim, it was profoundly crystal clear, and all four of us felt that exact same thing. Your brain was having trouble processing the clarity with which we were seeing this three-dimensional moon right there out of the window."

Spine-tingling stuff, even if here it was slightly off-topic, at least in an official capacity.

The premise of Wiseman's interview time with ESPN was not primarily about space. Although when you're talking to someone who has travelled a quarter of a million miles from Earth, how could it be about anything else?

Sitting at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, Wiseman was not wearing the orange spacesuit of Artemis II, nor the familiar dark blue of NASA, but the white of Mercedes' Formula 1 team's team kit. Six months after returning from his historic journey around the moon, Wiseman became an ambassador for the German manufacturer. Last year, he and his daughter had attended the United States Grand Prix on general admission tickets. Then, for all intents and purposes, Wiseman was just another person baking in the Texas sun with thousands of other people. Returning a year later he can boast that he's one of just nine living humans to have seen the far side of the moon with their own eyes.

The setting of the interview prompted an obvious question.

How does NASA compare to Formula 1? The answer was surprising.

"Oh, they crush us," he replied. "I mean, the level of engineering here, they smoke us."

Wiseman's view is rooted in the priorities of the two disciplines. NASA places a premium on proven technology and backup systems, even if that means carrying additional weight into space to ensure the mission objectives are met. Formula 1, meanwhile, is about the relentless pursuit of performance and pushing the boundaries of engineering in search of even the smallest advantage. As we spoke, we were surrounded by Mercedes' race operation -- engineers, mechanics, media team, performance coaches, who have impressed him as much as the technology.

"In spaceflight, what we really need is tried and true, redundancy, and we can accept a little bit of a mass penalty," he said. "Here, they're just pushing everything to the next level, and just every single thing is ... it's not just the cars, it's the humans. You know, everybody's walking around with WHOOP straps, and monitoring everything about themselves. They're all basically athletes. They're all going all in at all times. I love the way they deal with human performance and mechanical performance."

The competition aspect of Formula 1 -- which pits Mercedes against 10 other teams every race -- is always going to skew a comparison between Antonelli's world and Wiseman's world. For the Artemis II commander, it's the hunger to win that sets Formula 1 apart.

"At the end of the day in our work, there's a really large team of experts that sit just under the fanfare, but are the ones that are the true heroes that have the real courage. And then on top are these people who are willing to push the envelope a little bit and go.

"What is a little different for us is I have a crew of four people that are together in the spacecraft and working to try to make this mission the best it can be. In these cars, it is George [Russell] going all in, killer instinct ... Kimi [Antonelli] going all in, killer instinct. Occasionally they might meet in a corner and then I'm like, 'oh dear god, let's get through the corner.'"

For Mercedes, that focus on performance has seen the German team climb back to the pinnacle of the sport this year. Wiseman was speaking ahead of a U.S. Grand Prix which saw Kimi Antonelli move to the verge of becoming the sport's youngest-ever world champion at 20 years old.

This weekend, he will almost certainly wrap it up in Mexico City.

Wiseman can remember his interaction with Antonelli in 2024, before he had even started racing in Formula 1. Even then, Wiseman could see traits that have helped propel Antonelli to the brink of history.

"I met Kimi briefly when he was touring the Johnson Space Centre, and he invited me to a race when he was there," Wiseman said.

"[He was] 17. When I met him, the first thing I thought was how astonishingly humble and down to earth he was. But at the same time, he's a little goofy, which I love, but he's just curious about everything. We were touring with a few other drivers, but Kimi was asking every question about every single thing, whether he needed the information or not. Those are the people I try to latch on to because that curiosity is so powerful.

"You walk around, why is that cloud there? Why is that bird flying? How is it doing that? Why are these tyres better than these tyres?"

Antonelli's rise came after a rollercoaster rookie season in 2025. The young Italian has this year made a lot of the support network Mercedes put around him - team boss Toto Wolff's arm-over-the-shoulder approach to some of Antonelli's early mistakes were key. So has been the oversight of his race engineer, Peter Bonnington, who brought with him the experience of working in the same role with Lewis Hamilton.

Even here, Wiseman cannot help but point to where the two worlds overlap in some way.

"I chuckle at the way Bono and Kimi talk [on the radio]. It feels exactly like us in space, where we'll say something to the engineering team, and then when we unkey the mic, the engineering team will be like, 'they don't know what they're talking about', and then they'll come up with an answer for us, and they'll send it back. I love hearing that.

"I love it when the engineers and the drivers joke around on the radio, and you can just tell. It's just a great relationship."

Wiseman's link-up with Mercedes is a unique thing, but he feels right at home. He admits he was never one of those "crazy space kids" who could name every Apollo astronaut or had Neil Armstrong as a boyhood hero. But there was an interest in racing from a young age. He grew up going to NASCAR races with his father in Delaware, although they never did fulfill their dream of watching an Indy 500 together. His first chance to see Formula 1 in person was in 2023, invited by McLaren and Mercedes.

Wiseman admits he initially wondered what to expect from the "terrifying Toto Wolff," but has since come to admire the culture the Mercedes boss has established.

"What really struck me was, he's actually not scary, he's hilarious in his own humour. What I noticed as we were here, if you look around this place, there's no flash, it's just professionalism. 'We were going to go get the job done, and not just on the track.' It's the way they take care of the fans, the way they take care of the sponsors, the way they take care of the engineering team."

As he continued, Wiseman gestured over to Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti for another anecdote. "I went out for a run this morning with the engineers and did a swim down in Austin with them, and then I couldn't keep up on the way home, so I ran with Fred Vesti. He hung back and ran with me. The culture here always comes from the top. You can just tell Toto has one hell of a racing team that also knows how to take care of people."

Here is where he thinks NASA can learn a great deal from Formula 1's super-active team members. "Astronauts have to put a pretty good premium on our own health and physical conditioning, because we're going to be weightless, and our bones and our muscles are going to waste during the mission.

"So we put a big premium on that. We don't put as big of a premium on our support team and making sure they are at their highest level, and I think we can raise their level of expertise. They spend a lot of their days sitting in chairs, analysing data, and most of them would probably be upset if I said, let's go run three miles, but I think we can elevate the human performance, and we should really look at that. Because you look around in this team, everybody is fit, they're hungry, they're getting after it, and I think we can elevate the team [at NASA]."

Wiseman was brought to Mercedes to tell these kinds of stories. His role is to work with team partners, sponsors and guests to explain the overlap between the two worlds and, of course, to tell captivating stories about his own experiences. It's easy to see what he brings to the table. Had our interview not already overrun its 15-minute slot, it would have been easy to have kept going and going. "Toto likes the way I communicate," he said. "I think [guests] also like hearing stories of four humans that have gone further from Earth than anyone else. And I think there's just a lot of good storytelling and a sense of adventure that comes from that."

Inevitably, of course, our conversation drifted back to space.

Wiseman's anecdotes do not end with the stories he can tell verbally. At one point, he reached for his phone to show a picture with legendary Apollo-era flight director Gene Kranz, now 91, and Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise, taken earlier that week. Scattered through his camera roll were photographs he had taken himself of the moon from inside the spacecraft, through those smudged windows. Not a bad collection of snaps to have at your fingertips.

The Artemis II mission captivated a worldwide audience. In one of its most poignant moments, Wiseman's crewmates surprised him by naming a lunar crater in honour of his late wife, Carroll. But while millions of people followed their every move from Earth, the four astronauts were experiencing something rather different.

It is only since returning home that Wiseman has begun to appreciate just how much the mission meant to those watching.

"One thing that has been so rewarding is fame is not really that fun. I don't know how Kimi and George deal with that," he said. "But I was at an airport over in Europe the other day, and a dad came over to me and said, 'Hey, my daughter thinks you're Reid Wiseman. Are you?' And I said, yes, I am.

"And he turns to her, and this 10-year-old girl from the Philippines comes running over and just gave me the biggest hug. She knew everything about Christina, everything about Victor, everything about Jeremy.

"And I took this little medallion off my backpack and gave it to her, and she was so emotional. That stuff just is, it's all we could have ever wished for."

It was one of countless stories Wiseman and his crewmates have been hearing since they returned, providing a new perspective on a journey they are still coming to terms with themselves.

"We were all together three weeks ago. And we hadn't been together in a few weeks, and we were like, how's everything going? What are you feeling right now?

"And we all have this common feeling of we're starting to understand that we experienced this mission, but Earth experienced it. And now we're loving hearing the stories.

"Now that we've kind of processed the mission, we're listening to the stories from our friends at launch, when Carroll Crater was named, the amount of emotion that was involved in that. People were waking up and turning on the YouTube channel to see where are they today, what's going on.

"And we realised we went on a mission, but actually Earth kind of did too."

stories.headline: How Rays extended World Series in incredible Game 4 comeback
stories.summary: Milwaukee didn't get its sweep Tuesday night. Instead, the rest of the baseball world got a treat -- and another day to savor the sport.
stories.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida -- A long hibernation is coming to Major League Baseball, a winter of discontent, and so what happened here Tuesday night was deeply appreciated, a reminder of the game's unending ability to make us feel something. It is joy and it is pain and it is surprise and it is excitement and it is nausea and a million other things all at once.

"It's life," Yandy Diaz said.

The 35-year-old designated hitter was standing in the middle of the Tampa Bay Rays' clubhouse, still gobsmacked by what had unfolded over the previous 4 hours, 20 minutes, appropriate for a baseball game that left the Rays feeling plenty high. Their season looked dead, the World Series lost in embarrassing fashion, the Milwaukee Brewers ready to dogpile at Tropicana Field. Then the Rays remembered who they are at the precise moment they needed to, summoned the best of themselves and saved their season with a 4-3 victory in Game 4 that kept the Brewers from winning their first championship and ensured the Rays would live to see another day.

"We have tomorrow," Diaz said. "We have a new day. We have life."

Life coursed through the Trop on Tuesday. For the first three games of the Series, the Rays did not resemble the team that carved through the American League during the regular season and the playoffs. They played sloppy ball and committed uncharacteristic errors and looked entirely overmatched by a Milwaukee team brute-forcing its way into history. The Brewers had swept the Los Angeles Dodgers, and now they were going to do the same to Tampa Bay -- and nothing was stopping them.

Not after the top of Tuesday's 12th inning, when both teams had blown through their top relievers and Cooper Pratt stepped to the plate to face Rays left-hander Ian Seymour. Pratt is a 22-year-old rookie. He is from Mississippi, doesn't drink, doesn't curse. He just loves playing baseball. And on the first pitch he saw in the 12th, Pratt hammered it into the left-field stands, his fourth hit of the night, a backbreaking home run that left the Brewers half an inning from a championship the city of Milwaukee and the state of Wisconsin have spent 57 years trying to secure.

"I hit the thing and I was like, oh my gosh. That's gone," Pratt said. "I was just trying not to strike out. That was probably one of the coolest swings of my life."

Over the previous 11 innings, these two teams -- loaded with power arms, filled with speed, stocked with contact ability -- had gone back and forth in a tight, taut ballgame, and now the World Series was about to be won on the fourth hit of the day by a kid who wasn't even in the big leagues until June.

What's funny about the game, though, is its ability to take a remarkable moment and watch it get one-upped minutes later. That is life. That is baseball. That is feeling like you're on top of the world. That is the pain of tumbling from that perch into a pit of despair.

That pit, for the Brewers, started with what registers to the team as one of the more grievous sins: an error with no outs. Junior Caminero, the Rays' most dangerous hitter, rolled over a ground ball to third baseman Joey Ortiz, whose sure-handedness and reliability is matched by that of Jake Bauers at first base. Ortiz skipped the throw. Bauers couldn't pick it. And the tying runner was on base.

"I was just ... I don't even ... it's all kind of a blur at this point," said Rays catcher Liam Hicks, who followed Caminero by bouncing a single to left, leaving runners on first and third with no outs. "We've done this all year. We haven't this series, but it's always there."

When Rays outfielder Jonny DeLuca strode to the plate, the Brewers' infield came in -- and DeLuca smashed a Shane Drohan pitch right back up the middle. The score was tied. Then Chandler Simpson, the ultimate speedster, poked a ball up the chute to load the bases. Up came Ben Williamson, another pinch hitter deployed by Rays manager Kevin Cash, and Williamson did not hesitate.

One pitch. One swing. One improbable win.

"That's magic right there," Rays utilityman Ryan Vilade said.

Whether it was natural or supernatural, Tampa Bay found itself at the right time. The state of Wisconsin was preparing to drown itself with Miller Lite and Spotted Cow. And the Rays delayed the party for at least one more day.

"It was hard to sleep last night," Pratt said. "It's probably going to be a little harder tonight."

Outside of the Brewers clubhouse, outside of Wisconsin, the slumber following Game 4 would be nothing but glorious. As much as games like that imbue viewers and listeners and followers and die-hards and casuals alike with the reminder that nothing beats playoff baseball, they also take a chunk out of everyone. The ride is the joy. The ride is the pain.

And it's why, for anyone who's simply a fan of baseball, Game 4 resonated so deeply. On the one-year anniversary of the Dodgers and the Toronto Blue Jays' 18-inning World Series sojourn, Tuesday's Game 4 could have sent the sport into the coming lockout on a bitter note. Impressive though a sweep may have been for the Brewers, none of the previous games featured something as dramatic as Pratt's homer -- which was then one-upped minutes later.

Thankfully, baseball is still here, for at least one more day, before the cold realities of trying to grab as much money as possible shut down the sport for ... who knows how long? Game 4 was everything baseball is, everything baseball can be. It is, like Diaz said, life. And that life is being taken from you, sooner than later.

So, enjoy Game 5. It probably won't be as dramatic. It might crown a champion. It might send the World Series, improbably, back to Milwaukee. Baseball is the sport of infinite possibilities, of endless outcomes, and all it took was one game to remind us of that and to salvage the season for one more day.

stories.headline: NFL trade deadline grades: DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson dealt by Colts, more
stories.summary: Does Buckner make the 49ers Super Bowl hopefuls? Will Quenton Nelson upgrade the Seahawks' O-line? We're grading NFL trades ahead of November's deadline.
stories.body:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline, which is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

Here are our evaluations for the first deals of trading season, including the Colts sending guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

Jump to a trade:

Buckner | Nelson | Harrison

Jurgens | Porter | McCarthy

Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers

49ers get: DT DeForest Buckner

Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

49ers grade: A-

Colts grade: B-

As soon as the Colts emerged as a team that might engage in a trade-deadline teardown, it wasn't hard to see the dots connecting Buckner back to the 49ers. That became a reality Tuesday.

Though his numbers have dipped, Buckner, 32, can still help the 49ers get after the quarterback. He has four sacks this season, but his pass rush win rate ranked in the 45th percentile among defensive tackles, alongside a 69th percentile pressure rate. That is a drop from last season, when he was in the 90th and 88th percentile in those metrics, respectively. However, that 2025 performance is a positive sign for what he could bring to the 49ers the rest of this season.

Extra pass-rushing help will be welcome in San Francisco, which ranks 19th in pass rush win rate. The 49ers have been without Nick Bosa, who has been out because of a calf injury since Week 3 but is expected to return soon. Their pass defense is the only one of their major units (run and pass on offense and defense) that ranks outside the top seven in EPA per play (13th).

I'll admit I'm a little surprised the 49ers made this move considering they already have Osa Odighizuwa as a pass-rush-first defensive tackle. But he can play next to Buckner -- especially on passing downs. Also, San Francisco's rash of defensive line injuries makes any help welcome.

This type of roster-bolstering move makes sense for San Francisco. The 49ers are the Super Bowl favorites, according to ESPN's Football Power Index. In fact, they are the favorites by a lot, with the FPI giving them a 23% chance to win the Super Bowl (every other team is below 11%). Adding Buckner to reinforce those chances is worthwhile.

The cost was also quite reasonable. The 49ers are surrendering a fourth-round pick and taking over the prorated remainder of Buckner's $13 million salary, assuming his contract is untouched. While compensatory picks are never a guarantee, there's a decent chance that San Francisco might recoup most of that draft capital back via a comp pick if Buckner signs elsewhere in free agency next offseason, especially given that San Francisco is low on 2027 cap space.

That also is why I'm a little critical of the Colts' move here. Don't get me wrong, it absolutely makes sense for Indianapolis to trade him. The Colts are rebuilding, and Buckner is a 32-year-old in the final year of his contract -- of course they should have dealt him before the deadline.

Perhaps this was the best offer Indianapolis received for Buckner today, but they also didn't have to trade Buckner right now. There are two weeks left until the Nov. 10 trade deadline. I would have thought they could have at least squeezed another Day 3 pick in addition to the fourth-rounder. -- Walder

Colts trade G Nelson to Seahawks
Seahawks get: G Quenton Nelson

Colts get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

Seahawks grade: A-

Colts grade: B+

The reimagination of the Colts is officially underway, with longtime Indianapolis stalwart Nelson heading to the defending Super Bowl champions to bolster the interior of their offensive line.

Nelson, 30, started his career with three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. His level of play dropped in 2022 and 2023, but the 2018 first-round pick battled back to elite form in 2024, when he posted pass block and run block win rates that were each in the 90th percentile, along with earning second-team All-Pro honors. He earned a second-team All-Pro spot last season, too, along with a 91st percentile and 74th percentile pass block and run block win rates, respectively.

His win rates haven't been quite as strong this season (66th and 37th percentile, respectively), but Nelson's reputation is still superb, and having such consistent results the previous two years suggests he probably remains one of the best guards in the league if we're projecting the rest of the season.

The Seahawks presumably will keep Nelson at left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That will push Anthony Bradford, who recently returned from injured reserve and has played two games this season, to the bench. Bradford recorded 30th and 33rd percentile pass block and run block win rates last season, respectively, so Nelson is a substantial upgrade.

The Seahawks have Super Bowl aspirations but must get better play out of an offense that ranks 26th in EPA per play and 31st in EPA per designed rush. They rank 27th in run block win rate, 28th in yards per designed running back carry (3.6) and 28th in yards before contact on designed run plays. They also rank 21st in pass block win rate. So the team needed some offensive line help and upgrading their right guard or center made sense.

Nelson is on an expiring contract, so unless his deal was altered, the Seahawks will take on the prorated remainder of his $16 million in salary for this season, which is a bargain for the quality of play he brings. The Seahawks could sign Nelson to an extension or a new deal after the season, but they could also let him walk in free agency and possibly collect a compensatory pick to mitigate the draft capital lost in this trade.

It makes a lot of sense for the Seahawks to push their chips in on their current team. History tells us how hard it is to sustain elite defensive success, so the Seahawks need to take advantage while they have it.

This was also an easily logical move for the Colts. The 2026 season is lost, and Nelson is a pending free agent. Whatever value he would bring to the team in the second half of the season pales in comparison to what he brings to the Seahawks, and the draft capital return is more than they would get in compensatory picks (which are never a guarantee, anyway) had Nelson left in free agency. Plus, they save money on the remainder of his 2026 salary.

Ultimately, this is a win-win trade. Considering Seattle's contention window, positional (and overall offensive) need, the draft capital required and Nelson's contract, this is a sound move. -- Walder

Cardinals trade WR Harrison Jr. to Texans
Texans get: WR Marvin Harrison Jr., 2027 seventh-round pick

Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

Texans grade: C+

Cardinals: A-

Minutes after the Texans completed their 26-3 blowout win over the Titans, news broke that the rumored trade of Harrison, who was inactive Sunday because of the expected move, would be completed. The Cardinals sent him to Houston for a second-rounder and a sixth-rounder in 2027.

Similar to a lot of trades for young players, there are two simple questions: How much of our opinion of Harrison should be shaped by the league's predraft opinion of him and how much should be based on what we've seen from him in the NFL so far?

Harrison was considered a premier wide receiver prospect and was the first non-quarterback off the board with the fourth pick in the 2024 draft. But his production has fallen well short of those expectations to date, with Harrison amassing 1,578 receiving yards over 33 career games.

That equates to 1.5 yards per route run, which is in the 46th percentile among wide receivers who have run at least 15 routes per team game in that span. That number has been even worse in a small sample this season: just 0.6 yards per route run with a much higher percentage of deep fades and go routes (24%) than the previous two seasons (13%). Harrison's player-tracking metrics have been mediocre but not awful during his first two seasons: 47 and 54 overall in ESPN's receiver scores (with slightly better open scores) in 2024 and 2025, respectively.

Despite a rough start, the 1-4 Texans probably still believe they have a Super Bowl-caliber defense and a chance for a postseason run if they can get more talent around quarterback C.J. Stroud, who has been playing well. I don't think that's far-fetched despite their record. This is not the Texans' first attempt to upgrade at wide receiver. After second-year man Jayden Higgins suffered a torn ACL in August, Houston acquired Kayshon Boutte from the Patriots. But Boutte has managed only 1.1 yards per route run despite Nico Collins missing two games.

The Texans will get Harrison for cheap for the rest of this season and next year, and they will have a fifth-year option on him for 2028. But this move is not worth it if Harrison remains the same player he has been with the Cardinals because second-round picks have real value. Receivers who average 1.5 yards per route run can be found quite easily. The Texans are betting that Harrison can reach the upside he showed at Ohio State, including a breakout season in 2022 when Stroud was his quarterback. Having already played two-plus NFL seasons, the chances of a breakout aren't great, but they exist.

I think this trade makes sense for Arizona. The Cardinals didn't have to trade Harrison yet, but he will be worth more to a contending team than he is to them. It's likely his trade value would sink if they waited until the offseason to deal him. And Michael Wilson already had established himself as Arizona's No. 1 receiver.

Ultimately, I would not have made this trade if I were the Texans because the odds of Harrison breaking out immediately feel too low to justify the compensation. But I at least understand the thought process and desire to maximize a loaded roster's chances of making a real run to make the playoffs and win postseason games. -- Walder

Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens
Ravens get: C Cam Jurgens, 2027 seventh-round pick

Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Ravens grade: D+

Eagles grade: A

First, Tyler Linderbaum walked in free agency. Then the Ravens lost Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic to injury, suddenly leaving them without a center. Last week, Baltimore moved first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane to center but evidently doesn't see that as a long-term option.

So Baltimore turned to the trade market and dealt for Jurgens. It's an interesting and unusual move, because Jurgens is no stopgap. He's only 27 years old and is already on a long-term deal after signing an extension with the Eagles in 2025.

Jurgens moved from center to left guard in Week 2 after the Eagles placed guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve. It has not gone well. Jurgens ranks in the bottom three in both pass block and run block win rate at guard. But the Ravens are trading for Jurgens to have him play center.

In 2024, Jurgens was a Pro Bowl center who recorded pass block and run block win rates in the 80th and 50th percentiles, respectively. He made the Pro Bowl again in 2025, but his numbers slipped to the 65th and 39th percentile, respectively. He should be a stabilizing force for the Ravens -- perhaps an average to above-average center -- at what has suddenly become a position of need. But the cost is exorbitant.

The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He's due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens' $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer, per OverTheCap.com. By comparison, Connor McGovern, who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year.

One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens' salary is cheap this season. The Eagles have already paid Jurgens' option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary.

For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson. Jurgens hadn't played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall, who has played center after Jurgens' shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up.

I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday.

So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore's desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. -- Walder

Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys
Cowboys get: CB Joey Porter Jr.

Steelers get: 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Cowboys grade: B

Steelers grade: C+

This is the Cowboys' third trade with the Steelers in the past 18 months (George Pickens and Broderick Jones), and it's their third trade involving a star defensive player after acquiring Quinnen Williams at the trade deadline last season and shipping Micah Parsons to Green Bay last offseason.

It's easy to see what the Cowboys are doing here. DaRon Bland, who first broke onto the scene as a slot corner, was playing on the outside given Dallas' lack of depth. By acquiring Porter, Bland can move back inside, which will allow the Cowboys to relocate 2026 first-round defensive back Caleb Downs, as well. He has been playing the slot, but his natural position is at safety. These are options, not guarantees. Bland might stay outside as the Cowboys instead pursue a strong 1-2 punch at outside corner, with Porter shadowing WR1s.

The salient point is this: Porter can have a rising tide impact on the Cowboys secondary, clarifying the roles of other players and enhancing the whole unit in the process.

Porter is not as tricky of a scheme fit in Dallas as people think, too. His strengths are certainly his length and physicality, such that he can line up in press -- but he has been in press alignments on only 30.6% of his snaps over his career, just above the league average for cornerbacks (24.1%). Porter is a much better man coverage defender than he is in zone, as his passer rating allowed in man coverage over the past four seasons is better than all but Derek Stingley Jr. But the Cowboys are actually running more man coverage (24.8%) under first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker than the league average (23.2%) over the first three weeks.

Of course, early-season rate stats can be noisy. Parker's Vic Fangio-inspired defense will require Porter to play from greater depth than he did in Pittsburgh, and the communication and keys required in that match-heavy system will take some getting used to. But Porter has a valuable and rare skill set in his press-man ability, and premium picks should be spent on players with premium traits. The Cowboys got much, much better in the secondary -- though the move is not without risk.

Acquiring Porter does not solve all their deficiencies; linebacker is still a big problem for this team, and the edge rush isn't far behind. But if the secondary needs less schematic help now that Porter is in play, more coaching tools can be used to hide those other weak spots.

For the Steelers, Porter's recurring back ailments seemed incurable without an extension or a relocation -- what can you do? It's frustrating that GM Omar Khan invested more in third-contract players like Jalen Ramsey and T.J. Watt over a younger, second-contract player like Porter -- Ramsey and Watt will hit their athletic wall far sooner than Porter. Jamel Dean, another third-contract player signed to play corner opposite Porter, now has to cover WR1s alongside Asante Samuel Jr. and 2026 third-round pick Daylen Everette. Corner is no longer a strong position on Pittsburgh's depth chart.

Porter reportedly had contract demands up at the top of the cornerback market, where Devon Witherspoon and Christian Gonzalez recently reset elite deals to clear $33 million annually. I'm not sold that Porter is a top-tier corner deserving of that top money. But because the Steelers let this go on for so long and bleed into the regular season, they were only able to acquire a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for a young, ascendent cover corner. They could have -- and should have -- gotten at least a first-round pick by playing this differently and dealing Porter in the spring or earlier in the summer. -- Solak

Vikings trade QB McCarthy to Giants
Giants get: QB J.J. McCarthy

Vikings get: 2027 fifth-round pick

Giants grade: C

Vikings grade: B+

A mere 22 days after the Giants signed Jameis Winston to a two-year, $13 million extension, New York decided it needed to trade a fifth-round pick for an alternative at quarterback. Of course, a lot has happened in three weeks.

Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2 that is expected to keep him out for at least the regular season. And Winston has delivered two poor performances in Dart's stead, with a 19.0 QBR in relief in Week 2 against the Rams and a 27.9 in Sunday's 12-7 win over the Titans. So in comes McCarthy, the No. 10 pick in the 2024 draft.

McCarthy's pro career has gone poorly so far, which is putting it mildly. He suffered a season-ending knee injury in August 2024, which helped Sam Darnold become Minnesota's starting quarterback. McCarthy was named the starter last season after Darnold departed in free agency but started only 10 games after a series of injuries cost him time. And when he was on the field, the results were not good.

McCarthy posted a 36.1 QBR in 2025 (which ranked 38th out of 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts) and recorded a minus-5% pass rate over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats (43rd out of 45). He threw interceptions at a 4.2% clip (44th), took sacks on 9.4% of dropbacks (40th) and had a 1.8% fumble rate (41st). More alarming is that he did all that while playing for Kevin O'Connell, who has seemingly elevated most of the non-McCarthy quarterbacks he has called plays for.

During training camp, not only did McCarthy lose the Vikings' starting quarterback competition to Kyler Murray, but he then lost the backup competition to Carson Wentz, too. That is a telling red flag.

So why would the Giants trade for him? McCarthy presumably still has some upside based on his draft pedigree, and the Giants are hoping they can profit from him realizing it. But it's hard not to notice the fact that this is John Harbaugh trading for the quarterback his brother, Jim Harbaugh, coached in college at Michigan.

It is difficult to know from the outside which other backup quarterbacks would have been available, but McCarthy still does not seem like an ideal choice. Mac Jones and Spencer Rattler ought to have been the team's first calls (maybe they were). Kirk Cousins probably is off the board with the Raiders sitting at 3-0. Mitchell Trubisky might have been available, considering this already looks like a lost season for Tennessee. And I'm assuming Gardner Minshew II surely must be available, considering he sits in veteran no-man's land between Jacoby Brissett and rookie Carson Beck in Arizona. Stetson Bennett IV could have been an option, too, after the Rams selected Ty Simpson in the first round of this year's draft. I'll grant that some of those options have less upside than McCarthy.

But the Giants' front office should look in the mirror over its bungling of the Winston situation. It's not unreasonable for the Giants to be aggressive in finding a better replacement given how much time is left in the season. But they clearly shouldn't have signed Winston to an extension right before the season if this is how they feel about him!

Even though Murray is a free agent at the end of this season, McCarthy's ship had already sailed in Minnesota after he couldn't beat out Wentz. If he wasn't going to be the Vikings' backup quarterback, his value would likely have continued to drop. To get a fifth-round pick while saving a few million across his remaining 2026 and 2027 compensation (not nothing!) makes sense. They have uncertainty at quarterback in 2027, yes. But that was true whether McCarthy was there or not. -- Walder

stories.headline: Salkilld, Saint Denis to headline UFC Fight Night in Sydney
stories.summary: West Australian Quillan Salkilld will headline a UFC Fight Night lightweight matchup with Benoît Saint Denis in Sydney in February.
stories.body:
West Australian Quillan Salkilld will return to the Octagon in Sydney, after it was confirmed he'll headline the UFC Fight Night with a lightweight bout against Frenchman Benoît Saint Denis on February 7 (AEDT).

Salkilld, 26, is a former Australian rules footballer who turned to MMA after leaving school at 16, and boasts an impressive 13-1 professional record (6-0 in UFC) with five 'performance of the night' bonuses.

The Broome native has won four consecutive fights with a first-round finish, most recently submitting Mateusz Gamrot in their UFC Fight Night clash in Perth in August. He's widely regarded as Australia's next big combat star.

Meanwhile Saint Denis, 30, is one of the lightweight division's most dangerous finishers, and has a 17-4 professional record.

Peter Kloczko, senior vice president of UFC Australia and New Zealand, said the Fight Night -- to take place at Sydney's Afterpay Arena -- would be an "unforgettable event" featuring one of Australia's brightest young stars.

"UFC Fight Night Sydney is set to be another huge moment for Australian fans, and Quillan Salkilld versus Benoît Saint Denis is a main event that delivers everything we look for in this sport," he said in the official release.

"Quillan has been one of the breakout stars of the UFC's lightweight division, while Benoît is one of the most dangerous and exciting finishers in the sport. Bringing this fight to Sydney will make for an unforgettable night."

Further fights on the card will be released in due course.

stories.headline: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Ethan Drever has rocketed up draft boards
stories.summary: Growing up an Essendon supporter, Ethan Drever hasn't 'seen anything' like success. But his rise up draft boards could have him in the frame to be his childhood club's first pick, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Ethan Drever had absolutely no choice on his AFL team. As a newborn he was put in an Essendon jumper at the hospital and he's been a Bomber ever since.

It's been a rough 18 years of fandom since, and he's got some thoughts about his dad's decision.

"I'm [born in] 2008, I haven't seen anything!" he tells ESPN with a grin - and a grimace.

"Dad tells me about his success and I'm like, 'You don't have to rub it in like that.'"

The Dons are entering a new era in 2027 under Mark McVeigh and it's being driven through the draft. They snagged Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow, and Dyson Sharp in the first round 12 months ago and now own pick 1 in the upcoming draft.

Drever also has a lot of thoughts about those drafted before him.

"They've got some good young boys in there now. Robey, Sharp, they're gonna be so good.

"I like Farrow. He should be kicking in and doing all that, he needs to be in priority positions. That's what he's gonna be doing in the future.

"Just that halfback, I reckon he's gonna be really good... he's a beautiful left foot kick."

After a dour two-win season the Bombers have first call on Drever, with the 188cm on-baller strongly linked at the top of the board.

He's an electric runner with the intent to tackle, chase, and pressure - something that hasn't been a trait of Essendon's list for a long time.

Asked what he thinks when watching his boyhood club each weekend, Drever's response would prick the ears of all Bombers fans.

"It'd be nice to be out there and sort of help the boys out, that's kinda what I'm thinking!"

The Vic Country MVP and Rebels best and fairest produced a remarkable season. His star has risen from a first-round chance to the very top of the open pool.

He may have the most translatable traits to AFL level of any prospect. Drever is an elite power athlete, recording a 2.92 second 20 metre sprint which comes across in the tape. He bursts out of the contest with driving legs and loves to exit forward of the stoppage to inflict maximum damage.

His ultra consistent season has come about without any injury concerns, something all other top prospects this year haven't been able to say.

"It's been good not to have to sit on the sidelines this year at all and I can just keep playing consistent footy," he says.

"I only missed one [game] which was just after champs, I just had a break."

Drever lays claim to a pretty handy trademark. On six separate occasions this season he's collected the ball -- either out of a stoppage or in open play -- and powered away from opponents into the forward half of the ground.

From there his long running gait and elite top speed helps him separate from chasing defenders and break the paint of 50 to drive home sensational goals.

"I have heard it's called the trademark goal now. I don't know where that's really come from, it's just a natural thing I guess. I just like to run and have a ping from outside 50," Drever tells ESPN.

"Definitely one of my traits is just my power, especially this year. Building up over the pre-season and definitely my two-way running.

"It's the long-term goal to move into the midfield and be a bit of a Jordan Dawson with his two-way running. I love Finn Callaghan, how he plays. Those two are really great role models for me.

"I think Hugh McCluggage as well, I've watched him a lot. I had a meeting with him this year, he's that sort of two-way runner as well and he's been really good for me."

Drever played 13 games for the Rebels this year in amongst commitments with the AFL Academy and Vic Country. He collected the ball 28 times to go with a goal a game, but he's not satisfied with just being an offensive weapon.

The Ballarat local is a tenacious presence in contests with the appetite to chase and tackle, racking up 6.5 per outing to frank his status as the best pure midfielder in the open pool.

At the draft combine he showed off a much-improved engine running a 6:27 minute 2km after going 20 seconds slower in the lead-up. It's a time that will put him towards the front of the pack on day one of pre-season.

Drever knows exactly what's required to be a midfielder at the next level, and he's determined to get there as soon as possible.

"My endurance side was a big goal of mine, obviously at the top level you've just got to be able to run all day.

"Honing in on my fundamentals and trying to get them the best I can as well. That's what the most important thing is because it's the little one percenters that make a difference in the AFL.

Drever is now on the precipice of living out his dream of becoming an AFL player, and it could be for his boyhood club as the top choice in the open pool of the draft.

That won't matter to him, so long as he gets his opportunity to shine on the big stage.

"I don't really care [if I go at pick 1]. It's nice to have my name up in consideration alongside those boys but I'll just be happy to be picked up wherever I go."

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: Bafana boss Pitso Mosimane's latest South Africa squad shows favouritism fears were unfounded
stories.summary: Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.
stories.body:
When Pitso Mosimane returned as Bafana Bafana head coach, sceptics feared that his proximity to South African club football would lead to an erosion of the meritocratic culture Hugo Broos had built, but the 62-year-old's second preliminary squad suggests it has only been enhanced.

Mosimane began his tenure with Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea and a friendly victory over Egypt. Next up is the AFCON qualifying double-header against Kenya on Nov. 13 & 17.

Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.

Chicago Fire's Mbekezeli Mbokazi has returned from injury, while Aden McCarthy, Botiumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Luke le Roux, Thalente Mbatha, Nkosikhona Radebe, Devin Titus and Thakasani Mbanjwa have also received call-ups.

For every one of these call-ups, a layman can deduce a clear possible motive. McCarthy is the most obvious among them -- he has consistently featured at centre-back for Sabah in the UEFA Champions League and performed well at the highest level.

Radiopane and Xulu are in hot scoring form domestically for Orlando Pirates and Richards Bay respectively. Titus has earned his place with a strong start to life at MAS Fes in Morocco. Mbatha is back from injury and le Roux on the books of a new club at Cercle Brugge after struggling for game time at Portsmouth.

Radebe adds a right-back option from an in-form AmaZulu side with Mamelodi Sundowns' Khuliso Mudau still on the mend from injury. Mbanjwa is rewarded for a strong start to the season in goal for Golden Arrows.

Yanela Mbuthuma and Shandre Campbell -- both of whom have experienced dips in form and fortune at club level since the last international break -- are notable absentees.

In cutting two players he had given opportunities to after they had been mostly overlooked by Broos, Mosimane suggested he is willing to operate without fear or favour.

When 'Jingles' was on the verge of being appointed, Broos was quoted as telling Het Nieuwsblad: "You know, South Africa still don't have a coach. The candidate is Pitso Mosimane, a successful South African coach.

"But they know that if he comes in, they'll go five years back in time. Club owners and agents calling coaches to influence the squad selection. I threw all of them out. If one called, I would say bluntly: 'I don't talk with agents'."

The concern over agents and owners trying their luck in influencing the Bafana head coach may have been well-founded. Broos was not the first to complain of this within the national team setup.

However, questioning if Mosimane himself was open to influence without proof he was willing to make publicly available was ill-advised. It is impossible to accurately speculate on what conversations have or have not gone on between Mosimane and club owners and agents in the two months since then, but what is clear is that his team selection has been thoroughly meritocratic.

The momentum he has garnered is reminiscent of what Broos achieved in the first six months of his tenure.

At the time, the Belgian's irreverent team selection and approach to squad culture put everybody on their toes and led to an uptick in results. After they had failed to qualify for AFCON 2021 immediately before Broos was appointed, the Belgian fell narrowly short of steering Bafana into qualification playoffs for the 2022 World Cup.

In subsequent years, he kicked on and led Bafana to third place at AFCON 2023 (held belatedly in Ivory Coast in early 2024) and the 2026 World Cup round of 32.

When discussing the most successful Bafana Bafana coaches of all-time, Broos should be placed alongside Clive Barker in the top two. However, even the brightest tacticians eventually settle on patterns in their squad selection, and towards the end of his tenure, the Belgian became more predictable in certain aspects.

There was a fairly settled back five of Ronwen Williams, Aubrey Modiba, Mbokazi, Ime Okon and Mudau, and until he switched up his attacking plan to revive the FIFA World Cup campaign, Broos was likely to start Lyle Foster upfront with Evidence Makgopa the main alternative.

In midfield, Teboho Mokoena was a near certain starter and Sphephelo Sithole the clear preferred option alongside him, although Broos occasionally tinkered with his formation and left room for the likes of Bathusi Aubaas and the late Jayden Adams in the holding role. Nkosinathi Sibisi was considered another option, occasionally stepping out from the back into midfield.

Mosimane's arrival has reopened competition for places in these positions. Brooklyn Poggenpoel is retained in the squad after impressing in midfield over the last international break.

After Mbuthuma's minutes upfront, Radiopane and Xulu have been given a chance to earn theirs. Foster has made a second successive preliminary squad, although he failed to make the final squad last time out while in the process of leaving Burnley on loan to Houston Dynamo and settling in.

Fawaaz Basadien, Olwethu Makhanya, and McCarthy are in consideration in the backline. Mudau is, however, still the likely first-choice at right-back for the time being when he returns to full fitness. Still, Mosimane has done well to identify alternatives.

Mosimane declined to get drawn into a war of words with Broos over anything not directly related to matters on the pitch and instead praised his predecessor's impressive record as Bafana head coach.

In his first stint, Mosimane may not have succeeded in the hotseat. However, early results and his approach to team selection suggest he has justified the decision of the South African Football Association (SAFA) to give him a second chance and trust him to navigate the role without fear or favour to anyone.

Bafana Preliminary squad for Kenya (Nov. 13 & 17)
GK: Ronwen Williams, Sipho Chaine, Ricardo Gass, Thakasani Mbanjwa

DEF: Aubrey Modiba, Samukele Kabini, Fawaaz Basadien, Nkosikhona Radebe, Thapelo Morena, Thabang Matuludi, Olwethu Makhanya, Khulumani Ndamane, Ime Okon, Lebone Seema, Nkosinathi Sibisi, Mbekezeli Mbokazi, Aden McCarthy

MID: Teboho Mokoena, Lebohang Maboe, Sphephelo Sithole, Bathusi Aubaas, Brooklyn Poggenpoel, Thalente Mbatha, Luke le Roux

FWD: Iqraam Rayners, Cassius Mailula, Oswin Appollis, Tashreeq Matthews, Relebohile Mofokeng, Themba Zwane, Thapelo Maseko, Luther Singh, Devin Titus, Lyle Foster, Boitumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Tshepang Moremi, Puso Dithejane

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Flegler move likely; Cowboys keen to keep Nanai
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Flegler move looking likely
Tom Flegler is looking likely to leave the Dolphins at the end of 2027, with ESPN understanding the prop is leaning towards a move away from the club.

While Flegler is yet to make a firm decision, the Dolphins are now facing the prospect of losing him for the 2028 season and beyond.

His future shapes as a situation to watch as the November 1 contracting window approaches.

Cowboys keen to keep Nanai
North Queensland remain keen to retain Jeremiah Nanai, with ESPN understanding the Cowboys are hopeful the back-rower will extend his stay despite preparing to test his value on the open market from November 1.

Nanai has been with the club since he was a teenager, developing into a Queensland Origin representative, and the Cowboys are hopeful that connection will help keep him in Townsville.

Samrani expected to test open market
Jordan Samrani is expected to test the open market from November 1. ESPN understands he will explore his options for 2028 and beyond.

Following a breakout season with the Parramatta Eels, Samrani is open to assessing opportunities elsewhere when the contracting window opens on Sunday.

Cochrane set to link up with Titans feeder

Taye Cochrane is set to link up with Gold Coast Titans feeder club Ipswich Jets for the 2027 season following his departure from Canterbury.

ESPN understands the young fullback has signed with the Queensland Cup outfit after the Bulldogs opted against offering him a contract for next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances for Canterbury in 2026, having been part of the club's Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side in 2024.

The move follows Phil Gould's confirmation that Cochrane would leave the Bulldogs, with ESPN revealing he had not been offered a new deal.

Bulldogs opt against Cochrane deal

Canterbury have opted against offering Taye Cochrane a contract for 2027, with the young fullback set to depart Belmore.

ESPN understands Cochrane was not offered a new deal, following Phil Gould's confirmation he would not remain at the Bulldogs next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances this year, playing predominantly at fullback.

He was part of Canterbury's 2024 Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side before progressing to NSW Cup the following season.

Panthers make retention intentions clear on Patea
Penrith have informed Luron Patea's management of their desire to retain the young prop beyond 2027, although he still intends to test the open market from November 1.

ESPN understands multiple clubs are interested in speaking to Patea, who is approaching the final year of his Panthers contract.

ESPN previously reported that Penrith had yet to begin extension discussions with Patea.

Tigers keen to retain Mason

Wests Tigers are keen to retain Heath Mason, with the club working through roster space to accommodate the young utility.

ESPN understands Mason remains part of the Tigers' long-term plans, although his future is yet to be resolved ahead of 2027.

Cowboys open to keeping Taumalolo

North Queensland are open to retaining Jason Taumalolo beyond 2027, with the veteran forward's assessment of how his body is holding up set to guide the next step.

ESPN understands the Cowboys will take their lead from Taumalolo as he weighs up his playing future, reflecting his standing as a club legend.

Taumalolo is contracted until the end of next season and becomes eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 onwards from November 1.

Panthers lock in Patea
Penrith have secured Tua Patea until the end of 2029, with the youngster signing an extension that includes a pathway from a development contract into the club's top 30.

Patea capped off the 2026 season with a hat-trick in the Panthers' Jersey Flegg Grand Final victory, having started the year with an NRL training block.

The new deal will see him join Penrith's full-time NRL squad as he works towards a first-grade debut.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.

Formula 1 heads to Mexico on a weekend where Kimi Antonelli could win the drivers' championship for the first time.

The Mercedes driver extended his lead in the title to 123 points from George Russell after winning the United States Grand Prix. He will simply need to finish ninth or higher in Mexico City to seal the title.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was looking strong in the upgraded Ferrari to finish second in Austin, with Max Verstappen on the final step of the podium.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 19th round.

Mexico City is one of the most vibrant atmospheres on the calendar and fans congregate in the thousands to cheer on home hero Sergio Pérez.

It's a true anomaly on the calendar due to the high altitude of of 7,300 feet (2,200 metres) and therefore presents a unique challenge for the teams and drivers. Teams can run Monaco-level downforce packages while still reaching Monza-esque top speeds.

One of the iconic parts of the track -- the Foro Sol stadium section -- includes two tight corners in a former baseball stadium.

He had a one point advantage over Piastri with just four races to go.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli put his Mercedes on a surprise pole in Austin and converted it into another victory as he inches closer to taking the title crown with five races remaining.

The youngster will need just two points this weekend, or for Russell and Hamilton to not win the race, to get the job done in Mexico.

Red Bull are a looming threat each weekend after bringing major upgrades and Verstappen will be one to watch out for. He's also got five race victories under his belt around Mexico City.

All eyes will be on Antonelli. He will be hoping to wrap up the title and is looking like he's in a position where nobody will be able to stop him.

stories.headline: Arteta, Alonso, Iraola: Three Premier League managers all come from one tiny club
stories.summary: Whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or World Cup, hiring a coach from Spain's northern coast is bringing clubs guaranteed success.
stories.body:
There is irresistible evidence right now that signing coaching talent from Spain's northern coast brings guaranteed success, and Arsenal, Liverpool, Aston Villa and Chelsea need no convincing.

In international terms, the European and world champions (Spain) are coached by a Basque (Luis De La Fuente), in club terms, double Champions League winners PSG dance to the tune of another north-coast Spaniard, Luis Enrique, and the reigning Europa League holders and English champions owe their success to a couple of guys, Unai Emery and Mikel Arteta, who grew up within a few miles of one another in San Sebastián (part of the Gipuzkoa territory in Spain's Basque country).

It is, literally, a phenomenon. This is a coaching domination by a small community on a grand scale.

Now the fascinating prospect is that four of England's great clubs will all be jostling for trophies and bragging rights this season, in the Premier League and in Europe, under the control of coaches who all learned at one amateur Gipuzkoa football club on the Bay of Biscay coastline.

Arteta, Emery, Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso have already enjoyed jaw-dropping coaching success -- historic triumphs with Arsenal, Bournemouth, Bayer Leverkusen, Sevilla and Aston Villa between them. Now, they will all be going toe-to-toe for England's silverware.

What they also share, particularly Arteta, Iraola and Alonso, is an identical development path, often criss-crossing experiences in their home town of San Sebastián, being trained under the same ethos, often by the same coaches.

The amateur club in question is Antiguoko, which can claim partial responsibility for Bournemouth earning their first ever UEFA qualification (Iraola played for Antiguoko as a kid then, eventually, began his coaching career there), for Bayer Leverkusen winning their only Bundesliga title (Alonso) and for Arteta bringing Arsenal their first Premier League trophy in 22 years. Remarkable, right?

Those who run football at Antiguoko, and around the Gipuzkoa region, are beginning to smile with resignation as Europe's media approach them and demand the magic formula which has produced these brilliant alumni (and a host of other key figures in coaching and directorial roles around the continent).

There's no magic -- just ideology, hard work, decades of development and attention to detail.

Iraola says: "The number of successful coaches formed in the Basque Country receives a lot of attention because, despite being a small place, we have a great football culture."

When Arteta was last asked about what it is that makes Basque coaches so successful he gave a simple, short answer: "It's about passion we have and the education that we all got."

That education includes the fact that kids who follow the Arteta-Alonso-Iraola route in Gipuzkoa, aren't allowed to belong to a single club, practising a single sport, until they're 10 years or older.

The idea being that young boys and girls must continue to learn and develop through other sports like basketball, handball and volleyball before they, eventually, specialise.

The concept is to keep mixing with differently talented youngsters, to keep working on different spacial and athletic disciplines, to learn from and then cross-fertilise eclectic ideas.

Written down in black and white it makes simple sense, doesn't it?

There is also a huge emphasis placed on the coaches who train kids earning good qualifications, having a shared ideology, and being given respect by the community around them.

Again, doesn't that sound like basic common sense and decency?

During research for this column, Manu Diaz, the president of the Guipúzcoa Football Federation, explained: "There's a disproportionate number of coaches in our region because of our sense of community -- people want to give something back.

"Kids want to become coaches, they wait for their 16th birthday to be able to start doing their badges as if they were waiting for the chance to learn to drive. You also learn from a young age how to be part of a big group and that lends itself to eventually being good at leading. The coach is very well respected.

"People can invent a narrative that there is a common school of football here but really more than a shared way of seeing the game, it's a shared way of seeing life. There's a Basque word that sums it up: 'Auzolan' which refers to working together with neighbourly cooperation."

Some of that is evidenced by the way in which Arteta, Alonso, Iraola and co. learned their earliest football skills, and learned "neighbourly cooperation" via the phenomenon particular to San Sebastián where huge numbers of junior football matches are played on the two main beaches.

When the tide is out, parents, kids and coaches literally draw out a series of pitches on the flat, hard La Concha and Ondarreta sand, drag out stored goal-frames and play dozens of matches until the Cantabrian sea sweeps in again.

The pitch-lines need to be scraped out by hand in the sand. Speed and teamwork is of the essence -- not just when the matches start but in joining together to create the massive jigsaw of 10, 12, or 15 pitches as quickly as possible so that a host of games, with boys and girls of all ages, can take place. Teamwork makes the dream work.

Alonso, who won his first-ever trophy with Arteta in a tournament with Antiguoko when the pair were barely in their teens, explains: "I was lucky enough to have Mikel, who was also crazy about football, in our neighbourhood. Every day we'd go down to the beach on our skateboards to play tennis, surf, and, of course, play football."

There's no getting away from the fact that the Basque school of football development uses phrases and ideology which the modern, money-obsessed, fast-paced, hard-nosed elite world of football would find hokey and old-fashioned.

Perhaps that's the key: All the things that drive old-school fans crazy, that make them feel detached from the modern, foreign-owned, exorbitantly priced, corporate and investment-fund football are the opposite to the Antiguoko, Gipuzkoa, Basque ways which gave us Alonso, Arteta, Iraola and Emery.

"It shines a spotlight on one of European football's premier youth academies," an Antiguoko spokesperson told ESPN. "We are a neighbourhood institution -- modest in resources yet colossal in influence. We have served for decades as a true school for both footballing and human development.

"These guys who now work in the Premier League have publicly acknowledged the profound impact Antiguoko K.E. had on their athletic and personal development. We nurture players, by fostering raw talent, but also via a culture of hard work, tactical intelligence, game interpretation, and collective commitment.

"A footballing philosophy grounded in competitiveness and holistic development. Our club embodies the very essence of local grassroots football. Here, football is in the air from a very young age -- but so, too, are discipline, a sense of closeness, and a deep feeling of belonging."

Five years ago Alonso was one of the co-authors of the Real Sociedad training manual, "Made In Gipuzkoa" published to help anyone across global football who cared to read it, learn from it and apply the concepts.

One of its key phrases, again sounding from another age, is: "The essence of this model is the person, not just the footballer."

The training manual continued: "That boy or girl whose future we don't yet know -- footballer, engineer, doctor, mechanic, lawyer -- is the centre of everything. In this model, each person is a project in themselves, and everything else revolves around them.

"Coaches at Real Sociedad accompany, nurture, and train the boys and girls throughout their entire journey, with stability as the foundation of a model based on trust and patience. In short, to nurture, to train, to guide, to educate. That is the mandate we receive from the community we want to represent, from the families of Gipuzkoa, from Gipuzkoa society in general."

From that old-fashioned, humanistic, community-based football philosophy to the cutthroat, high-tech winner-takes-all ebb and thrust at the top of England's Premier League.

Whatever divides Alonso, Emery, Arteta and Iraola this season, they are all unified by background, beliefs and some values that all of European football could learn from.
